title: Intense Heat May Be Linked to Climate Change
main_content:
A massive heat wave is killing people in many countries around the world.

Most die of heat stroke. Heat stroke is the most serious heat-related sickness. It can develop when body temperature reaches 40.5 degrees Celsius (or 105 degrees Fahrenheit).

Victims need water and other cooling measures.

A heat wave in Pakistan will join this year’s heat wave in India as one of the 10 deadliest in world history. Extreme heat has killed more than 1,500 people in Pakistan. Temperatures in areas of India and Pakistan have reached as high as 47 degrees Celsius.

For Pakistan, seasonal rains are expected to begin in the middle of this month which will cause temperatures to drop.

But Europe does not have a similar rainy season to help break the extreme heat. Millions there may continue to suffer temperatures as high as 40 degrees Celsius.

Omar Baddour is a climate expert at the World Meteorological Organization. He says it is too early to link the current heat waves to man-made climate change.

Extreme heat is also affecting southwestern and southeastern China.

questions.question: When can heat stroke develop?
options: When body temperature exceeds 39 degrees Celsius
When body temperature reaches 40.5 degrees Celsius
When hydration levels are significantly low
When exposure to sunlight lasts for more than two hours
questions.answer: When body temperature reaches 40.5 degrees Celsius

questions.question: What does Europe not have that could help break the extreme heat?
options: A significant number of cooling centers
A prolonged rainy season to lower temperatures
Access to international aid for heat relief
questions.answer: A prolonged rainy season to lower temperatures

questions.question: Who is Omar Baddour?
options: A meteorologist studying future heat patterns
A climate expert at the World Meteorological Organization
The director of a global heat relief charity
A government official in charge of disaster responses
questions.answer: A climate expert at the World Meteorological Organization
